study.title: 2 Kings 10 - Jehu executes judgment on the house of Ahab, and eliminates the worship of Baal, but walketh not with the whole heart before the LORD.
study.overview: The chapter shows Jehu advancing on two fronts: first, he eliminates Ahab's descendants and allies, consolidating the throne of Israel violently; then destroys the institutional cult of Baal in Samaria. In both cases, the text insists that this fulfills the word of the Lord dictates through Elijah. However, the narrative also makes a point of showing the limit of Jehu's reformation: he removes Baal, but preserves the sins of Jeroboam, especially the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. Thus, the king receives partial approval for obeying in part, but his faithfulness remains incomplete, and divine judgment still falls upon Israel through Hazael. The chapter ends by highlighting the duration of Jehu's reign and the continuity of the dynasty for four generations, in contrast to the spiritual fragility of the kingdom.

outline.title: Threat to the survivors of Ahab's house
outline.explanation: Jehu sends letters to Samaria, challenges the leaders to defend the dynasty of Ahab if they really want, and shows that resistance is useless. The leaders yield out of fear, and the seventy children of Ahab are killed. Jehu then interprets the fact as fulfillment of the word of the Lord pronounced by Elijah, shifting the focus of the political scene to divine judgment.

outline.title: Expansion of the massacre and alliance with Jonadab
outline.explanation: Jehu continues to eliminate all that was left of Ahab's house, including relatives of Ahaziah of Judah. Then finds Jonadab the son of Rechab and invites him to witness his zeal for the Lord. The passage suggests cooperation between the reform of Jehu and the approval of a godly man, although the text does not declare that this makes Jehu fully faithful.

outline.title: The destruction of Baal in Samaria
outline.explanation: Astothing, Jehu summons all the servants of Baal to a solemn assembly, make them look like their ministers, isolate the temple and send them out. Then he overthrows the idols and transforms the temple of Baal into latrine, officially ending this cult in Israel. The narrative underlines that idolatry is extinguished from the public sphere, although Jehu's method is deceptive and violent.

outline.title: The incomplete fidelity of Jehu and the decline of Israel
outline.explanation: Despite removing Baal, Jehu does not abandon the sins of Jeroboam and continues with the worship of the golden calves. The Lord approves him only in relation to what he did against the house of Ahab, promising dynastic continuity until the fourth generation, but also begins to reduce the territory of Israel through Hazael. The chapter closes with the death of Jehu, the succession by Jehoahaz and the duration of his reign, twenty-eight years.

study.context: The text takes place in the kingdom of the North, Israel, with the administrative capital linked to Samaria and the other important scene in Jezreel. The chapter itself indicates that Ahab's house still had survivors, guards and allies, which shows that the change of power was still underway. The religious background is the dispute between the worship of the Lord and the worship of Baal, in addition to the persistence of the golden calves established by Jeroboam. The notes also presuppose the prophetic word given earlier by Elijah about the judgment against the house of Ahab.
study.theology: The chapter strongly affirms God's sovereignty over history: the fall of Ahab's house does not happen by chance, but according to the word of the Lord. At the same time, the text distinguishes between instrument and moral model. Jehu is used to execute judgment, and the Lord recognizes this, but his obedience is partial and his heart does not appear fully turned to the law of God. This teaches that God can use imperfect people to fulfill their purposes without approving all the way they act. The narrative also shows that destroying an idol does not automatically equate true spiritual reform; removing Baal is not enough if the previous sins remain active. There is therefore judgment, partial faithfulness, and the principle that the outer zeal without an entire covenant with God remains insufficient. Israel's territorial decline functions as a sign of cursing the infidelity to the alliance.

scholarViews.insight: Jehu acted beyond the divine commission by killing all the survivors of the house of Ahab; the comment sees it an excess and not just obedience.
Jehu received divine approval for what he did against Ahab's house, but the commentary points out that his spiritual progress did not correspond to the promising beginning of the reign.
The commentaries point out that Jehu's letters were ironic and aimed to intimidate the leaders of Samaria, revealing the political intention behind the speech.

questions: What does the text teach about the difference between being an instrument of God and being an example of complete faithfulness to God?
Why did Baal not enough to say that Israel had been spiritually restored?
How do the fear of Samaria's leaders and Jehu's cunning shape the moral reading of this chapter?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to examine whether his obedience to God is partial or whole. It is not enough to reject a visible idol if other sins remain accommodated. It also teaches not to confuse success, strength, or external results with full approval from God. In practice, this means asking the Lord not only for the courage to fight what is wrong, but also a whole heart to walk in his law. When reading Jehu, the Christian is invited to value the truth of God more than the very impulse to overcome or appear as zealous.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow us to state that Jeú is presented with partial approval and also with criticism of his excesses, but do not allow to safely detail his internal motivations beyond what the text and commentators say. The chapter also does not clarify, in itself, all the subsequent consequences of Jehu's reform; this would require other texts. I kept the historical context restricted to what the chapter itself and the notes support, without expanding with external data not provided.
